<reason>Both sides were competent and format-compliant, but CON (A) made the decisive clash easier to decide. A's "missing middle" informal-worker frame survived the whole debate: PRO's defenses required a "near-universal launch that tightens later" and an admission that "compensation before the shock was never on the menu," and A converted both into concessions that the motion delivers a certain price shock with contingent relief. A also answered PRO's strongest pressure (the symmetry question) directly, reframing Nigeria and Iran as the motion being executed rather than subsidies failing on their own—a reframe PRO only reasserted against rather than dismantled. PRO's regressivity arithmetic was blunted by the share-of-income reply, and its "fiscal space for clinics" was effectively cast as a hope versus tomorrow's pump price. PRO's best material—subsidies detonate when money runs out, categorical targeting without registries—was real but not developed enough to overturn A's sequencing argument, and A's "trim/phase slowly" line, while slightly self-undermining, was not exploited. PRO also had more clipped turns.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's A1 in Rebuttal 2: turning PRO's symmetry demand around by arguing Nigeria's "collapse" was a government announcing removal with promised transfers that stalled—i.e., the proposition in action—paired with seizing PRO's "never on the menu" concession to frame the choice as certain loss versus contingent relief.</best_rebuttal>
